label: Fragile relief
summary: The world climbs nine points to 43 — its best reading in weeks and back into the 'Mixed' band — because the war that has driven the mood all month stopped, at least for a night. The United States held off striking Iran for a third consecutive evening after 13 straight nights of bombing, and Tehran suspended its retaliatory attacks in return; Trump said talks were under way and he hoped for 'good things,' though Iran's foreign ministry insisted there are 'no negotiations with the United States at present.' Markets read the pause as real: Brent crude fell to below 88 dollars and US crude to about 82, a drop of roughly nine percent, and Wall Street closed higher with the Dow up 0.53 percent to 52,485.03, the S&P 500 up 0.70 percent to 7,489.72 and the Nasdaq up 1.00 percent to 25,373.85 despite a memory-chip selloff. The relief is fragile. Drones still flew: Saudi Arabia intercepted attacks on Riyadh and its eastern oil facilities, satellite imagery appeared to show damage at the Abqaiq processing complex claimed by Yemen's Houthis, and drones were downed over Israel, Jordan and northern Iraq. Europe carried the day's worst news. Wildfires around Bordeaux and central Spain have forced roughly 220,000 people from the Gironde, 30,000 more from the Landes and over 100,000 in Madrid, Toledo and Ávila, with President Macron calling the crisis 'completely unprecedented' and the toughest France has faced since the Second World War. Russia and Ukraine traded barrages that killed at least ten people, including a nine-year-old girl in a Chernihiv supermarket, and Romania recalled its ambassador from Moscow and expelled a Russian diplomat after four drone incursions into NATO airspace in four days. Elsewhere the ledger stayed heavy: Pakistan's monsoon toll passed 100 with 107 dead and 344 injured; RSF drones hit El-Obeid hours after Sudan's army reopened the highway to Khartoum; DR Congo's Ebola outbreak surged to 3,200 cases and 1,405 deaths, up about a thousand infections in ten days; and a pit collapse at the Gold Ridge mine on Guadalcanal left at least ten informal miners feared dead. The brighter column was genuine: Israel freed 60 Palestinian detainees to Gaza, the largest release since October's ceasefire; the Gordie Howe International Bridge opened between Detroit and Windsor, the first new crossing there in a century; UNESCO inscribed the Amazon opera houses of Manaus and Belém as World Heritage sites; the FDA approved a second blood-based colorectal cancer screening test; and astronomers reported the first plausible detection of a moon beyond our solar system. Also on the day: Berlin police shot dead the suspect in the Pride car-and-machete attack that killed one and injured 29, and Hurricane Genevieve became 2026's first Category 5 in the eastern Pacific, forecast to stay clear of land. The headline matches the rubric formula with no adjustment.

drivers.headline: The United States pauses air strikes on Iran for a third consecutive night after 13 straight nights of bombing, and Iran halts its retaliatory attacks in return, in the first sustained lull of the Gulf war; President Trump says the US is in talks with Tehran and hopes for 'good things,' but Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei counters that there are 'no negotiations with the United States at present' and that Iran 'will never allow the United States to determine the timing of war and peace'

Drone attacks spread across the region despite the US-Iran lull: Saudi Arabia's defence ministry says it intercepted drones launched from Iraq by Iran-backed militias at petroleum facilities in the Eastern Province and around Riyadh, and satellite imagery circulating online appears to show damage and a large plume of smoke at Saudi Aramco's Abqaiq processing plant, the world's largest; Israel and Jordan each shoot down two drones near the Dead Sea, drones hit camps of Iranian Kurdish opposition forces in northern Iraq, and the Houthis claim strikes on oil transit sites feeding the Red Sea port of Yanbu

Oil prices collapse and US stocks rally as the pause in US-Iran hostilities holds: crude tumbles roughly nine percent, with Brent falling below 88 dollars a barrel and US benchmark WTI to about 82, unwinding much of the war premium that had carried Brent above 100 dollars last week; the Dow closes up 276.97 points or 0.53 percent at 52,485.03, the S&P 500 gains 0.70 percent to 7,489.72 and the Nasdaq adds 1.00 percent to 25,373.85, with Apple overtaking Nvidia as the world's most valuable company even as SanDisk and Micron slump on memory-chip weakness, ahead of a Federal Reserve decision and results from Microsoft, Meta, Apple and Amazon later in the week

Wildfires burning across southwestern France and central Spain force one of the largest evacuations in modern French history, with roughly 220,000 people cleared from the Gironde since the main fire broke out last week, at least 30,000 more from the Landes and over 100,000 ordered out in the Spanish regions of Madrid, Toledo and Ávila; President Emmanuel Macron calls the crisis 'completely unprecedented' and the toughest France has faced since the Second World War, with 116,085 hectares already burned nationally this year across 13,566 recorded fire starts and crews racing another heat wave

Russia and Ukraine trade attacks that kill at least ten people, after Russia launches seven ballistic missiles and 136 drones overnight at Kyiv, Chernihiv, Zaporizhzhia and Kharkiv: a drone strike on a Chernihiv supermarket kills two including a nine-year-old girl and wounds 25, a daytime attack on Kharkiv kills one and injures 16, a glide bomb kills one in Zaporizhzhia, and two Naftogaz workers die in Sloviansk, while Ukrainian drones kill four civilians in Russian-held Horlivka and injure 12 in Belgorod; US-led peace talks remain stalled, and the spillover reaches NATO as Romania recalls its ambassador from Moscow and expels a Russian diplomat after downing three drones in its airspace between 24 and 26 July

Pakistan's monsoon death toll passes 100, with the National Disaster Management Authority reporting 107 killed and 344 injured since late June — 55 dead in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and 36 in Punjab — and more than half the deaths caused by collapsing houses and roofs; about 400 square kilometres are submerged across the Lahore and Gujranwala divisions where 17 relief camps have opened, and the meteorological department warns a fresh wet spell will begin Wednesday across upper Punjab, Kashmir, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Gilgit-Baltistan with the season still only at its midpoint

Rapid Support Forces drones strike El-Obeid at dawn, destroying the local lawyers' association and a branch of the Agricultural Bank of Sudan with no casualties reported, hours after Sudan's army pushed the RSF west off the 400-kilometre highway linking the city of some 500,000 people to Khartoum; UN figures show drone strikes by both sides have killed more than 1,000 people in Kordofan alone since January, in a war that has killed an estimated 200,000 since April 2023 and left over 33 million needing aid in the world's largest displacement and hunger crisis

DR Congo's Bundibugyo-virus Ebola outbreak surges to 3,200 confirmed infections and 1,405 deaths, an increase of roughly a thousand cases in ten days, with the virus now present in five provinces including two newly affected and almost 90 percent of cases concentrated in northeastern Ituri; strikes by health workers over unpaid wages are disrupting the hospital response, and while Oxford University has begun trialling an experimental vaccine against the Bundibugyo strain, no approved vaccine or treatment yet exists for it

A ground collapse at Pit 1 of the Gold Ridge mine in central Guadalcanal, Solomon Islands, buries informal miners in the early hours of Monday, with local outlet In-depth Solomons reporting at least ten bodies recovered and excavators still clearing earth in search of others believed trapped; the victims were unauthorised gold panners rather than company employees, in the third such fatal incident at the site since 2023

Israel releases 60 Palestinian detainees into Gaza, the largest single release since the prisoner exchanges under October's ceasefire, with the Israeli military saying those freed are not considered 'terrorists'; the Red Cross facilitates the handover at the Kerem Shalom crossing and the men are taken to Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital in Deir al-Balah and the Nasser Medical Complex, where the Palestinian Prisoners' Media Office says the health of many had deteriorated in captivity

The Gordie Howe International Bridge opens to traffic over the Detroit River, linking Interstate 75 in Michigan with Highway 401 in Ontario — the first new vehicle crossing between Detroit and Windsor in about a century and now North America's longest cable-stayed span, with a main span of 0.53 miles, towers 722 feet high and 216 stay cables, after eight years of construction and two decades of planning; the celebration was muted, with Canada cancelling the joint ribbon-cutting and US officials absent amid the trade dispute, and a supply-chain scholar noting that 'one of the biggest challenges is going to be how to repair relationships'

UNESCO's World Heritage Committee, meeting in Busan, inscribes the Theaters of the Amazon on the World Heritage List in the early hours of Monday — the Teatro Amazonas in Manaus with the Largo de São Sebastião and the Theatro da Paz in Belém with the Praça da República — the first Amazonian theatres ever to receive the designation; both were built at the height of the rubber boom, Theatro da Paz opening in 1878 and Teatro Amazonas in 1896, and the listing extends Brazil's heritage recognition beyond its southern and coastal cities

The US Food and Drug Administration approves Freenome's SimpleScreen CRC, a blood-based colorectal cancer screening test for average-risk adults aged 45 and over, giving clinicians a second approved blood option; the PREEMPT CRC trial across more than 200 sites and some 48,000 asymptomatic participants found 81.1 percent sensitivity for colorectal cancer and 90.4 percent specificity, with Abbott to commercialise it in the US this autumn — one of several science bright spots on a day when researchers using the Very Large Telescope reported in Nature the first plausible detection of an 'exosatellite' orbiting a brown dwarf in the CD-35 2722 system
